sections.text: Many languages use null to mean "no value", and forgetting to check for it causes crashes. Rust has no null. Instead it has the enum Option:

Option<i32> means "an Option that may hold an i32". In the definition, T stands for any type, so you can have Option<String>, Option<bool> and so on. The same angle-bracket notation appears in Vec<i32> and HashMap<char, i32> later. Unit 7 explains it fully.
A function that might not have an answer returns an Option. The caller has to deal with both cases before using the value:

Handy helpers: unwrap_or gives the value, or a fallback if there's none. is_some and is_none tell you which case you have. To use the value only when it's there, you'll use match or if let, coming in the next lesson.
unwrap() stops the program if the value is None. It's fine in quick experiments, but prefer unwrap_or, match or if let in real code.

Option<T> is generic over T. Many collection methods return it, e.g. get on a Vec (really a slice method), Iterator::next, str::find. Combinators like map, and_then and ok_or let you chain transformations without unwrapping.

exercise.prompt: first_even returns an Option. Finish even_or_zero so it returns the first even number, or 0 if there is no even number, using first_even and unwrap_or. For [3, 7, 8, 10] main should print: 8

tests.label: Takes the first even number, not the last

hints: even_or_zero must give back a plain number, but first_even gives back an Option, which may hold a number or nothing.
Option has a method unwrap_or that takes a fallback value. Call first_even(numbers) and then .unwrap_or(0) on its result.
Replace todo!() with first_even(numbers).unwrap_or(0) and no semicolon, so it is the value the function returns.

quiz.question: What are the two variants of Option?
quiz.explanation: Option has the variants Some (a value is there) and None (no value). Ok and Err belong to Result, and Rust has no True and False variants, because bool is its own type.

quiz.question: What does Rust use instead of null?
quiz.explanation: Rust has no null. When a value might be missing, you use Option, and the compiler makes you handle the None case before you can use the value inside. A 0 or an empty string could be mistaken for a real value.

quiz.question: What does None.unwrap_or(5) give?
quiz.explanation: unwrap_or(5) gives the value inside Some, or 5 when there is nothing. Since this is None, you get 5. It doesn't crash, which is what unwrap would do.
